levels.title: First steps with Copilot
levels.focus: The three Copilot surfaces, persistent instructions, and reusable prompt files — the foundations every developer needs.

quiz.prompt: In VS Code, which Copilot surface can read your workspace, create several files in one turn, and propose a global diff you accept or reject?
options: Inline suggestion
Copilot Chat
Agent mode
The Copilot status bar icon
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is right because agent mode can inspect the workspace, create or edit multiple files, and present one global diff for review. Option 0 is wrong because inline suggestions mainly complete code in the currently open file and do not orchestrate multi-file changes. Option 1 is wrong because Copilot Chat can explain or propose code, but it does not by itself apply a workspace-wide diff. Option 3 is wrong because the status bar icon indicates connection/status, not a code-generation surface.

quiz.prompt: "Use Vitest, never Jest" must apply to every conversation in your repo. What is it?
options: A prompt — restate it in each request
A persistent instruction, e.g. in .github/copilot-instructions.md
A skill triggered by the semantic router
An MCP server setting
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is right because a repository-wide rule belongs in a persistent instruction file that Copilot loads for every chat and agent interaction. Option 0 is wrong because a prompt is a one-time request and would have to be repeated. Option 2 is wrong because a skill is conditional procedural know-how, not an always-on convention. Option 3 is wrong because MCP settings configure executable external tools, not team coding preferences.

quiz.prompt: Which file do Copilot Chat and agent mode load automatically for every conversation in a repository, with no activation step?
options: .vscode/copilot.json
.github/copilot-instructions.md
README.md
.agents/instructions.md
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is right because .github/copilot-instructions.md at the repository root is the shared instruction file loaded automatically by Copilot Chat and agent mode. Option 0 is wrong because .vscode/copilot.json is not the documented repository instruction file. Option 2 is wrong because README.md may be useful project documentation, but it is not automatically treated as Copilot instructions. Option 3 is wrong because .agents/ is used for agents and skills, not the global instruction file.

quiz.prompt: You want TypeScript-only rules that load only when a .ts file is in scope. What does the handbook recommend?
options: Add the rules to README.md
Create .github/instructions/typescript.instructions.md with an applyTo: '**/*.ts' frontmatter
Put every language's rules in one big copilot-instructions.md
Rename the file to typescript.prompt.md
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is right because scoped instruction files under .github/instructions/ use applyTo globs to load only for matching files. Option 0 is wrong because README.md is not the mechanism Copilot uses for scoped instructions. Option 2 is wrong because a large global file bloats context for conversations that do not involve TypeScript. Option 3 is wrong because a .prompt.md file is a manually launched command, not an automatically scoped instruction.

quiz.prompt: In a .prompt.md file, which mode should you pick for a command that explains code but must never modify files?
options: agent
edit
ask
chat
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is right because ask mode answers in chat without modifying files, which fits explanation-only tasks. Option 0 is wrong because agent mode can read, write, and run commands, making it too permissive for a no-edit command. Option 1 is wrong because edit mode is designed to modify the open file. Option 3 is wrong because chat is not one of the documented .prompt.md mode values.

quiz.prompt: Which VS Code extension recommendations does the setup module add so a repo nudges developers to install Copilot support?
options: GitHub.copilot and GitHub.copilot-chat
ms-python.python and GitHub.copilot
GitHub.vscode-pull-request-github and dbaeumer.vscode-eslint
Only GitHub.copilot-chat
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is right because the setup module recommends both GitHub.copilot and GitHub.copilot-chat in .vscode/extensions.json. Option 1 is wrong because the Python extension is unrelated to the Copilot setup shown. Option 2 is wrong because pull request and ESLint extensions do not provide the three Copilot surfaces. Option 3 is wrong because Copilot Chat alone omits the core Copilot extension.

quiz.prompt: What is the best use case for an inline suggestion according to the setup module?
options: Creating a whole test suite across multiple files
Calling an MCP server to list GitHub issues
Writing repository-wide instructions
Completing local, trivial code in the open file and accepting with Tab
quiz.explanation: Option 3 is right because inline suggestions are intended for local completions in the currently open file, commonly accepted with Tab. Option 0 is wrong because multi-file test generation is a better fit for agent mode. Option 1 is wrong because MCP tool calls belong to agent/tool workflows, not inline completion. Option 2 is wrong because repository instructions are written in files, not produced by the inline surface.

quiz.prompt: You have repeated the same convention in several Copilot conversations. What rule of thumb from the instructions module applies?
options: Move it to an instruction if you repeat it more than twice
Keep it as a prompt forever
Convert it to an MCP server
Put it only in OBSERVATIONS.md
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is right because the handbook says a rule repeated across conversations deserves a persistent instruction. Option 1 is wrong because repeating the prompt wastes effort and risks inconsistency. Option 2 is wrong because MCP is for executable tools and external data, not static behavior rules. Option 3 is wrong because OBSERVATIONS.md is an exercise artifact, not an automatic Copilot context mechanism.

quiz.prompt: Where should reusable .prompt.md files be placed so the team can launch them from the VS Code command palette?
options: .github/instructions/
.agents/skills/
.github/prompts/
.vscode/extensions.json
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is right because reusable prompt files live in .github/prompts/ and appear as commands in VS Code. Option 0 is wrong because .github/instructions/ is for scoped .instructions.md files. Option 1 is wrong because .agents/skills/ contains SKILL.md procedures, not prompt files. Option 3 is wrong because extensions.json recommends extensions and does not define Copilot commands.

quiz.prompt: Which frontmatter keys are described as controlling a .prompt.md file's behavior?
options: name, trigger, model
applyTo, severity, timeout
servers, command, env
mode, description, and optionally tools
quiz.explanation: Option 3 is right because the prompt frontmatter documents mode, description, and an optional tools list. Option 0 is wrong because name and trigger are not the prompt-file keys described in the module. Option 1 is wrong because applyTo belongs to scoped instructions, while timeout is a hook concept. Option 2 is wrong because servers, command, and env are MCP configuration fields.

quiz.prompt: Which .prompt.md variable asks the user for a value when the prompt is launched?
options: ${file}
${input:name}
${selection}
#file:path/to/file
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is right because ${input:name} opens a VS Code input prompt and injects the user's answer. Option 0 is wrong because ${file} resolves to the active file content rather than asking a question. Option 2 is wrong because ${selection} injects selected editor text. Option 3 is wrong because #file:path/to/file references a specific file, not an interactive input.

quiz.prompt: Which .prompt.md mode is most appropriate when Copilot should refactor a targeted portion of the currently open file in place?
options: edit
ask
agent
manual
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is right because edit mode is designed to modify the open file in place for focused changes. Option 1 is wrong because ask mode only replies in chat and will not edit. Option 2 is wrong because agent mode is broader than necessary for a targeted in-place refactor. Option 3 is wrong because manual is not a documented .prompt.md mode.

quiz.prompt: What does #file:path/to/file do inside a reusable prompt body?
options: It creates a new file at that path
It limits the prompt to files matching a glob
It injects the referenced file's content into context
It sets the prompt's execution mode
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is right because #file:path/to/file is used to reference a specific file and provide its content as context. Option 0 is wrong because file creation requires an appropriate mode and tool, not a #file reference. Option 1 is wrong because globs for loading rules are handled by applyTo in instruction files. Option 3 is wrong because execution mode is set in frontmatter with mode.

quiz.prompt: Why is using agent mode for every reusable prompt an anti-pattern?
options: It prevents prompts from appearing in the command palette
It forces all prompts to become instructions
It disables variables like ${selection}
It adds unnecessary latency and tool calls when no file changes are needed
quiz.explanation: Option 3 is right because agent mode is powerful but slower and tool-heavy, so explanation-only prompts should use ask. Option 0 is wrong because prompts can still appear in the palette when their frontmatter is valid. Option 1 is wrong because mode does not convert a prompt into an instruction. Option 2 is wrong because variables are a prompt feature and are not disabled merely by choosing agent mode.

quiz.prompt: How does the instructions module recommend proving that a new instruction is actually active?
options: Run the same prompt before and after the instruction and compare the observable behavior
Assume it works once the file exists
Restart GitHub.com
Rename the instruction to README.md
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is right because the module recommends comparing the same prompt before and after to see a concrete delta such as Vitest instead of Jest. Option 1 is wrong because file presence alone does not prove the instruction affected a response. Option 2 is wrong because GitHub.com is not the VS Code chat session that loads the instruction. Option 3 is wrong because README.md is not the instruction filename Copilot automatically loads.

levels.title: Skills, agents, and hooks
levels.focus: Teach Copilot procedural know-how, build custom conversation agents, and automate on agent events.

quiz.prompt: What determines whether Copilot loads a skill stored in .agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md?
options: The skill is loaded in every conversation, like an instruction
The semantic router matches the skill's description against the user's request
The user must type the skill name in the prompt
The skill loads whenever its folder is open in the editor
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is right because the skill description is the semantic trigger Copilot compares with the user's request. Option 0 is wrong because instructions load every conversation, while skills load conditionally. Option 2 is wrong because users do not have to type the folder or skill name for model-invoked skills. Option 3 is wrong because opening a folder in the editor is not the activation mechanism.

quiz.prompt: A procedure is only needed when someone asks for a commit message, but a style rule must apply everywhere. How do you split them?
options: Both as skills
Both as instructions
Commit procedure as a skill, style rule as an instruction
Commit procedure as an instruction, style rule as a skill
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is right because commit-message writing is a conditional procedure, while a style rule is persistent context. Option 0 is wrong because a style rule should not depend on a semantic trigger. Option 1 is wrong because loading the commit procedure in every conversation wastes context. Option 3 is wrong because it reverses the handbook's distinction between always-on rules and on-demand procedures.

quiz.prompt: How do you build a review-only agent (.agent.md) that cannot modify files or run commands?
options: Add 'read-only' to its description
Set model: gpt-5-mini
Omit editFiles and runInTerminal from its tools list
Set mode: ask in the frontmatter
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is right because the tools list is the enforcement lever: tools not listed are unavailable to the agent. Option 0 is wrong because a description is guidance, not a hard capability boundary. Option 1 is wrong because changing the model does not remove file-editing or terminal tools. Option 3 is wrong because .agent.md uses tools and persona frontmatter, not a prompt-file mode field.

quiz.prompt: Agent A delegates to agent B with runSubagent. What context does B receive?
options: A's full conversation history
B runs isolated with its own tools and model — only what A explicitly passes
Everything in A's context window plus the workspace
B shares A's tool permissions automatically
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is right because a sub-agent runs in an isolated sub-conversation with its own frontmatter configuration and only the transmitted task context. Option 0 is wrong because the delegated agent does not automatically see the caller's full history. Option 2 is wrong because the context window is not blindly copied into the sub-agent. Option 3 is wrong because the sub-agent keeps its own tool permissions rather than inheriting the caller's.

quiz.prompt: Which hook mechanism can block a dangerous tool call before it executes?
options: PostToolUse with decision: 'block'
SessionStart with additionalContext
PreToolUse returning permissionDecision: 'deny'
Stop with a reason
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is right because PreToolUse fires before execution and can return permissionDecision values such as deny. Option 0 is wrong because PostToolUse runs after the tool has already completed, so it cannot prevent execution. Option 1 is wrong because SessionStart adds initial context but is not tied to a pending tool call. Option 3 is wrong because Stop can ask the agent to continue after a response, not block a tool in advance.

quiz.prompt: What are the three parts of the skill mechanism emphasized by the handbook?
options: When, what, and how
Model, token budget, and temperature
Prompt, completion, and cache
Server, tool, and transport
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is right because a skill defines when it triggers, what it is called, and how Copilot should proceed. Option 1 is wrong because those are model configuration concerns, not the anatomy of a skill. Option 2 is wrong because prompt, completion, and cache describe LLM interaction mechanics rather than skill structure. Option 3 is wrong because server, tool, and transport are MCP concepts.

quiz.prompt: What is the canonical location for a skill named writing-commit-message?
options: .github/prompts/writing-commit-message.prompt.md
.github/instructions/writing-commit-message.instructions.md
.agents/writing-commit-message.agent.md
.agents/skills/writing-commit-message/SKILL.md
quiz.explanation: Option 3 is right because each skill lives in its own folder under .agents/skills/ with a SKILL.md file. Option 0 is wrong because .github/prompts/ stores reusable prompts, not skills. Option 1 is wrong because .github/instructions/ stores scoped instruction files. Option 2 is wrong because .agent.md files define custom agents, not conditional skills.

quiz.prompt: Why are many vague skills a problem even if they are not selected for a conversation?
options: The semantic router must evaluate them and vague descriptions pollute routing signal
They automatically overwrite .github/copilot-instructions.md
They disable all agents in the workspace
They force Copilot to use MCP
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is right because the router evaluates skill descriptions and too many vague triggers create noise. Option 1 is wrong because skills do not overwrite the repository instruction file. Option 2 is wrong because the presence of skills does not disable custom agents. Option 3 is wrong because skills are text procedures and do not force MCP usage.

quiz.prompt: Which frontmatter fields are required for a basic .agent.md according to the agents module?
options: applyTo and mode
name and description
servers and env
hook_event_name and timeout
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is right because an agent needs a name and description so it can appear and be understood in the mode selector. Option 0 is wrong because applyTo is for scoped instructions and mode is for prompt files. Option 2 is wrong because servers and env belong to MCP configuration. Option 3 is wrong because hook_event_name and timeout belong to hook payloads and hook definitions.

quiz.prompt: In an .agent.md file, what is the difference between omitting tools and setting tools: []?
options: Both make the agent read-only
Both give the agent no tools
Omitting tools gives no tools; tools: [] gives all tools
Omitting tools gives all available tools; tools: [] gives no tools
quiz.explanation: Option 3 is right because no tools key leaves the agent with all available tools, while an explicit empty list grants none. Option 0 is wrong because omitting tools is not read-only. Option 1 is wrong because only tools: [] removes all tools. Option 2 is wrong because it reverses the documented behavior.

quiz.prompt: What should you do with an old .chatmode.md customization in this learning path?
options: Migrate it by renaming to .agent.md and checking the frontmatter
Create new .chatmode.md files for every role
Move it to .vscode/mcp.json
Convert it into a hook script
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is right because the agents module treats .chatmode.md as obsolete and recommends migrating to .agent.md. Option 1 is wrong because the module says not to create new .chatmode.md files. Option 2 is wrong because mcp.json configures executable MCP servers, not chat personas. Option 3 is wrong because hooks are event scripts, not conversation modes.

quiz.prompt: Which hook event can inspect and enrich a user's message before the agent processes it?
options: PostToolUse
SubagentStop
PreCompact
UserPromptSubmit
quiz.explanation: Option 3 is right because UserPromptSubmit fires when the user submits a prompt, before the agent processes it. Option 0 is wrong because PostToolUse occurs after a tool call, not before prompt handling. Option 1 is wrong because SubagentStop fires when a sub-agent finishes. Option 2 is wrong because PreCompact is about conversation-history compaction, not prompt filtering.

quiz.prompt: What must a hook configuration JSON contain at its root, and how are event names written?
options: A prompts array and snake_case events
A hooks object and PascalCase event names
A servers object and lowercase event names
A tools list and kebab-case event names
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is right because hook files contain a root hooks object and events such as PreToolUse are written in PascalCase. Option 0 is wrong because prompts arrays are not the hook schema and snake_case event names are not documented. Option 2 is wrong because servers is the root key used by MCP configuration. Option 3 is wrong because tools lists are agent or prompt concepts, not the root hook schema.

quiz.prompt: How can a command hook report a blocking failure through its process result?
options: Exit with code 2 and send the blocking message on stderr
Exit with code 0 and print nothing
Exit with any nonzero code and rely on VS Code to guess
Return YAML on stdout only
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is right because the hooks module specifies exit code 2 as blocking, with stderr returned to the model. Option 1 is wrong because exit 0 means success and does not block by itself. Option 2 is wrong because other nonzero codes are warnings, not the documented blocking path. Option 3 is wrong because hooks communicate structured data as JSON, not YAML.

quiz.prompt: When multiple hooks respond to the same event, which control wins?
options: The fastest hook wins
The machine hook always wins
The most restrictive control wins
The hook with the shortest filename wins
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is right because the handbook states that when several hooks respond, the most restrictive control takes precedence. Option 0 is wrong because timing is not the precedence rule. Option 1 is wrong because workspace hooks have priority in loading, but response conflict resolution is about restrictiveness. Option 3 is wrong because filenames do not determine hook decisions.

levels.title: Tools and models
levels.focus: Extend Copilot with MCP servers without compromising security, and pick the right model for each task.

quiz.prompt: Why does the handbook say "never connect an MCP server you haven't audited"?
options: MCP servers slow down inline completions
An MCP server is an executable process running with your permissions — it can read files, run commands, or exfiltrate secrets
MCP servers overwrite copilot-instructions.md
MCP servers only work with one model family
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is right because an MCP server is a real executable process with the permissions and secrets you give it. Option 0 is wrong because the primary warning is about security, not inline-completion speed. Option 2 is wrong because MCP servers do not inherently overwrite Copilot instruction files. Option 3 is wrong because MCP is a protocol for tools and is not limited to a single model family.

quiz.prompt: What is the recommended way to give an MCP server a GitHub token in .vscode/mcp.json?
options: Hard-code the token in the env block
Use ${input:github-token} so VS Code prompts for it
Commit the token in .env
Paste the token in the chat once per session
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is right because ${input:github-token} prompts locally in VS Code and keeps the shared configuration free of secrets. Option 0 is wrong because hard-coded tokens can be committed and leaked. Option 2 is wrong because committing a token in .env is still committing a secret. Option 3 is wrong because pasting secrets into chat is not a safe or reusable MCP configuration mechanism.

quiz.prompt: You keep 5 MCP servers with 10 tools each connected. What is the hidden cost even when you never use them?
options: Nothing — unused tools are free
50 tool descriptions are injected into the system prompt on every request
Each server charges a per-minute fee
VS Code disables inline completions
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is right because connected MCP tools add their descriptions to Copilot's context each turn, consuming tokens and adding noise. Option 0 is wrong because unused connected tools still have context overhead. Option 2 is wrong because the handbook discusses token/context cost, not per-minute server billing. Option 3 is wrong because MCP connections do not disable inline completions.

quiz.prompt: According to the GitHub task categories, which models should you pick for deep reasoning and debugging?
options: Raptor mini and GPT-5 mini
Claude Haiku 4.5
GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro, or Goldeneye
Any model — they are equivalent
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is right because the model-choice module places those premium reasoning models in the deep reasoning and debugging category. Option 0 is wrong because Raptor mini and GPT-5 mini are better framed as general or lighter choices, not the main premium debugging set. Option 1 is wrong because Claude Haiku 4.5 is recommended for fast simple tasks. Option 3 is wrong because the module explicitly differentiates models by task category, quality, speed, and cost.

quiz.prompt: Why is "one model per session" the recommended rule?
options: Model switching is not allowed by license
Switching invalidates the prompt cache prefix, producing inconsistent results and re-billing tokens at full price
Different models cannot read the same files
Sessions crash when models change
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is right because switching models breaks the prompt-cache prefix and can make results less consistent while increasing token cost. Option 0 is wrong because the rule is about efficiency and coherence, not licensing. Option 2 is wrong because different models can access the same provided context and files through Copilot. Option 3 is wrong because the handbook warns about cache and consistency, not guaranteed crashes.

quiz.prompt: When should you prefer MCP over a skill?
options: When Copilot must execute an external tool or API call to obtain real data
When you want a permanent style rule
When you need a short procedure for commit messages
When you only want to reduce prompt wording
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is right because MCP gives Copilot executable tools that can fetch real data from APIs, files, or networks. Option 1 is wrong because permanent style rules belong in instructions. Option 2 is wrong because a commit-message procedure is the handbook's classic skill example. Option 3 is wrong because reducing prompt wording is better handled by reusable prompts or skills, not necessarily executable MCP servers.

quiz.prompt: Which fields describe the minimal stdio GitHub MCP server command in .vscode/mcp.json?
options: applyTo, mode, description
name, tools, model
hooks, command, timeout
type: stdio, command, args, and env
quiz.explanation: Option 3 is right because the MCP example declares a stdio server with a command, arguments, and environment variables for the token. Option 0 is wrong because applyTo, mode, and description belong to instructions or prompt files. Option 1 is wrong because name, tools, and model are .agent.md frontmatter concepts. Option 2 is wrong because hooks, command, and timeout describe hook configuration rather than MCP server startup.

quiz.prompt: If an official CLI can perform the same action as an MCP tool, what does the handbook generally recommend?
options: Use the native CLI through the terminal
Always install the MCP server anyway
Write the result by hand
Disable agent mode
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is right because the handbook says native CLIs such as gh, az, git, or kubectl often have lower token cost, lower latency, and a smaller attack surface. Option 1 is wrong because unnecessary MCP servers add context overhead and third-party process risk. Option 2 is wrong because manually fabricating results defeats the purpose of grounded tooling. Option 3 is wrong because agent mode can run terminal commands and does not need to be disabled.

quiz.prompt: Which setting value makes VS Code ask for confirmation before every MCP tool call?
options: once
never
always
auto
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is right because chat.mcp.toolCallConfirmation set to always requests confirmation for every tool call. Option 0 is wrong because once confirms only once per tool per session. Option 1 is wrong because never disables confirmation and is reserved for trusted servers. Option 3 is wrong because auto is not one of the documented values for this setting.

quiz.prompt: Which token practice best matches the MCP security guidance?
options: Use an admin:org token by default
Commit a shared team token in a private repo
Give every server the same broad token
Use the smallest scopes needed and avoid storing the secret in the repo
quiz.explanation: Option 3 is right because least privilege and not committing secrets are central MCP security practices. Option 0 is wrong because admin:org is far broader than needed for most tasks. Option 1 is wrong because private repositories can still leak secrets and committed tokens are hard to rotate safely. Option 2 is wrong because broad shared tokens increase blast radius if a server is malicious or compromised.

quiz.prompt: What does Auto mode in the VS Code model picker do?
options: Routes each request based on task complexity and model availability
Forces the cheapest model for every task
Disables model choice in custom agents
Uses only visual-capable models
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is right because Auto evaluates the request and real-time availability to select an appropriate model. Option 1 is wrong because Auto is not defined as cheapest-only routing. Option 2 is wrong because custom agents can still specify a model in frontmatter. Option 3 is wrong because Auto is not limited to visual-input tasks.

quiz.prompt: How do you force a specific model for a custom agent?
options: Put the model name in .vscode/extensions.json
Add model to the skill description
Set the model key in the .agent.md frontmatter
Use applyTo in .github/instructions/
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is right because .agent.md frontmatter supports an optional model key for roles that need a particular model. Option 0 is wrong because extensions.json recommends extensions and does not configure agent models. Option 1 is wrong because skill descriptions are semantic triggers, not model selectors. Option 3 is wrong because applyTo scopes instructions to files and does not choose language models.

quiz.prompt: What is thinking effort in the model-choice module?
options: A way to count how many files an agent edited
A replacement for MCP tool confirmation
A setting available on every non-reasoning model
A configurable amount of reasoning applied by supported reasoning models
quiz.explanation: Option 3 is right because thinking effort controls how much reasoning supported models apply to a request. Option 0 is wrong because it is not an edit-count metric. Option 1 is wrong because tool confirmation is a separate MCP safety setting. Option 2 is wrong because non-reasoning models such as GPT-4.1 do not show the thinking-effort submenu.

quiz.prompt: How do chat model selection and inline completion model selection relate in VS Code?
options: They are independent and can be changed in different UI paths
They must always be the same model
Inline completions are billed exactly like chat tokens
Changing chat models disables completions
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is right because the module explains that chat and inline suggestion models are configured separately. Option 1 is wrong because they are not required to match. Option 2 is wrong because code completions and next-edit suggestions are not billed in AI credits for paid plans. Option 3 is wrong because changing the chat model does not disable inline completions.

quiz.prompt: Under the 2026 usage-based pricing described in the model module, what drives the cost of a Copilot interaction?
options: Only the number of requests
Only whether the repo is public or private
The model used and the number of input, output, and cached tokens
The number of VS Code extensions installed
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is right because the module says cost depends on the selected model and token usage, including input, output, and cache. Option 0 is wrong because the module describes a move away from request-based billing. Option 1 is wrong because repository visibility is not the pricing driver discussed. Option 3 is wrong because installed extensions do not determine AI credit consumption.

levels.title: Composition at team scale
levels.focus: Package, share, and orchestrate primitives with APM, multi-agent workflows, plugins, and the Copilot CLI.

quiz.prompt: In an APM setup, where does the exact resolved commit SHA of each dependency live?
options: In apm.yml next to each dependency
In apm.lock.yaml (resolved_commit + content_hash), generated automatically
In .github/copilot-instructions.md
Only in the Git tag
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because APM resolves dependencies into apm.lock.yaml, recording resolved_commit and content_hash for reproducible installs. Option 0 is wrong because apm.yml is the declarative manifest and may pin a tag, but it does not store the resolved SHA. Option 2 is wrong because .github/copilot-instructions.md is compiled output for Copilot, not the dependency lock state. Option 3 is wrong because a Git tag can move or be absent, while the lockfile records the exact commit actually installed.

quiz.prompt: Which command makes APM-installed primitives visible to VS Code / Copilot?
options: apm audit
apm run copilot
apm compile -t copilot
apm publish
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is correct because apm compile -t copilot writes the compiled Copilot configuration, such as .github/copilot-instructions.md, that VS Code can read automatically. Option 0 is wrong because apm audit checks installed content and drift, but it does not generate Copilot-facing instructions. Option 1 is wrong because scripts are run with apm run only if defined; this is not the standard compilation command. Option 3 is wrong because publishing makes primitives available to others, not visible to the local Copilot client.

quiz.prompt: In an Outside-In workflow, why must the orchestrator explicitly pass sub-agent N's output to sub-agent N+1?
options: To keep an audit log
Because sub-agents run in isolated conversations and never see previous steps' history
Because sub-agents only accept JSON
To avoid exceeding the model's rate limit
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because each sub-agent has its own isolated context, so the orchestrator must relay only the needed result to the next step. Option 0 is wrong because audit logging may be useful, but it is not the reason context must be passed. Option 2 is wrong because sub-agents can receive natural-language or structured inputs; JSON is not the constraint. Option 3 is wrong because rate limits are unrelated to the handoff of information between isolated conversations.

quiz.prompt: What defines a Copilot plugin, compared with installing individual primitives via APM?
options: A plugin is a paid binary from a store
A plugin is a bundle of skills/agents (manifest .github/plugin/plugin.json) installed as a block, e.g. from github/awesome-copilot
A plugin only works in JetBrains IDEs
A plugin is another name for an MCP server
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because a Copilot plugin packages a coherent set of primitives with a .github/plugin/plugin.json manifest and is installed as a unit. Option 0 is wrong because plugins are Git-distributed primitive bundles, not necessarily paid binaries. Option 2 is wrong because the module describes VS Code / Copilot plugin installation, not JetBrains-only behavior. Option 3 is wrong because an MCP server is an external tool process, whereas a plugin can contain skills, agents, hooks, and possibly MCP configuration.

quiz.prompt: In the terminal, which command asks Copilot to explain an unfamiliar shell command flag by flag?
options: gh copilot suggest -t shell
gh copilot explain
gh explain
copilot --help
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because gh copilot explain takes an existing command and breaks down its program and flags in natural language. Option 0 is wrong because suggest generates a command from an intention rather than explaining a command you already have. Option 2 is wrong because gh explain is not the Copilot CLI subcommand taught in the module. Option 3 is wrong because a help command lists usage information, not a flag-by-flag explanation of an arbitrary shell command.

quiz.prompt: What is the strongest reason to commit apm.lock.yaml alongside apm.yml in a team repository?
options: It stores the APM CLI binary for offline installation
It guarantees each clone resolves the same dependency commits and content hashes
It replaces the need for .agents/ directories
It makes Copilot ignore local primitives
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because the lockfile records resolved commits, content hashes, and deployed files, giving every developer a reproducible configuration. Option 0 is wrong because the lockfile does not contain binaries or install APM itself. Option 2 is wrong because APM deploys primitives into agent directories; the lockfile only records what should be deployed. Option 3 is wrong because Copilot visibility is controlled by compiled configuration and installed primitives, not by ignoring local content.

quiz.prompt: Which dependency string is the handbook's canonical shape for an individual APM primitive?
options: owner/repo/kind/name
kind:name@owner/repo
https://github.com/owner/repo#kind=name
owner.repo.kind.name
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is correct because APM dependencies use the path-like form owner/repo/kind/name, for example anthropics/skills/skills/frontend-design. Option 1 is wrong because colon and at-sign notation is not the manifest format shown in the handbook. Option 2 is wrong because full URLs are not the canonical dependency string for primitives, even though GitHub hosts the repositories. Option 3 is wrong because dotted package names are not how APM locates primitives inside a repository.

quiz.prompt: When is the handoff workflow pattern preferable to an Outside-In orchestrator?
options: When the workflow is a simple linear chain with no branching or feedback loops
When each agent must see the entire conversation history
When the root agent must inspect every intermediate token
When sub-agents need unrestricted tools at every step
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is correct because the handbook presents handoff as lighter for linear A → B → C chains where each agent passes its result to the next. Option 1 is wrong because handoff still passes only the needed result, not the entire history. Option 2 is wrong because a root agent inspecting every step is characteristic of central orchestration, not handoff. Option 3 is wrong because workflows should still keep each agent's tools scoped to its responsibility.

quiz.prompt: In the issue-to-code workflow example, why does spec-writer not receive editFiles?
options: Because GitHub issues cannot be read by agents
Because the orchestrator writes specs directly
Because its responsibility is to return specification text, not modify the workspace
Because editFiles only works after tests pass
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is correct because spec-writer has a single responsibility: read issue context and produce a structured spec without side effects. Option 0 is wrong because the example gives spec-writer GitHub access specifically to read issue information. Option 1 is wrong because the orchestrator is explicitly forbidden from doing the work itself. Option 3 is wrong because editFiles is a capability choice, not something gated by test results.

quiz.prompt: What file does a Copilot plugin manifest use to declare its name, version, keywords, agents, and skills?
options: .agents/plugin.yml
.github/plugin/plugin.json
apm.lock.yaml
installed.json
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because the plugin anatomy in the handbook centers on .github/plugin/plugin.json for metadata and paths to agents and skills. Option 0 is wrong because .agents/plugin.yml is not the manifest path described for Copilot plugins. Option 2 is wrong because apm.lock.yaml belongs to APM dependency resolution, not plugin metadata. Option 3 is wrong because installed.json records installed plugins locally after installation rather than defining the plugin itself.

quiz.prompt: Why is project scope often safer than user scope for a stack-specific Copilot plugin?
options: Project scope gives the plugin more file-system permissions
Project scope disables the plugin's skills until VS Code restarts
Project scope keeps stack-specific descriptions from polluting unrelated workspaces
Project scope converts the plugin into an APM package
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is correct because a project-scoped plugin is active only in the current workspace, reducing irrelevant router candidates elsewhere. Option 0 is wrong because the point of scope is availability, not automatically granting more permissions. Option 1 is wrong because the handbook does not frame project scope as a restart-based disabling mechanism. Option 3 is wrong because scope selection does not change a plugin into an APM dependency.

quiz.prompt: Before installing a third-party plugin, which security check best matches the handbook's guidance?
options: Trust it if the plugin has many keywords
Install first, then audit only if Copilot behaves strangely
Read the SKILL.md and .agent.md files and verify requested tools match the advertised function
Prefer plugins without version tags because main is always freshest
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is correct because plugin content runs in the agent context, so source review and tool-scope review are essential before installation. Option 0 is wrong because keywords improve discovery, not trustworthiness. Option 1 is wrong because the handbook recommends auditing before exposing the agent to potentially dangerous instructions. Option 3 is wrong because tagged versions are safer than mutable main branches for reproducibility.

quiz.prompt: Which Copilot CLI flag narrows gh copilot suggest to Git commands?
options: --mode git
-t git
--git-only
-x git
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because the CLI module documents -t git as the type selector for Git command suggestions. Option 0 is wrong because --mode git is not the flag shown for gh copilot suggest. Option 2 is wrong because --git-only is not the documented selector. Option 3 is wrong because -x git is not part of the taught Copilot CLI syntax.

quiz.prompt: What is the main drawback of a monolithic do-everything agent in the workflow chapter?
options: It cannot call GitHub APIs
It saturates one context with unrelated instructions and overly broad tools
It forces every sub-agent to return XML
It prevents any testing command from running
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because the monolithic agent mixes specs, planning, coding, and broad tools in one conversation, making context noisy and debugging difficult. Option 0 is wrong because the example super-agent can include githubRepo access. Option 2 is wrong because no XML return format is required by the workflow pattern. Option 3 is wrong because the monolithic example may run tests; the problem is scope and context, not inability to execute commands.

quiz.prompt: What is installed.json in the Copilot plugin installation model closest to?
options: A package-lock-style record of installed plugins and their sources
The source manifest that plugin authors commit
The file that stores APM resolved_commit values
A transcript of every skill invocation
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is correct because installed.json records which plugins are installed with their pluginUri and marketplace source, supporting environment reproducibility. Option 1 is wrong because authors commit plugin.json, not installed.json, as the plugin manifest. Option 2 is wrong because resolved_commit values are part of APM's lockfile, not Copilot's plugin install record. Option 3 is wrong because installed.json tracks installations, not runtime skill activations.

levels.title: Pipelines, LSP, and evals
levels.focus: Run rigorous multi-agent pipelines, wire compiler-grade LSP intelligence, and prove skill value with binary and LLM-judge evals.

quiz.prompt: In the handbook's writing pipeline, why must the reviewer agent start with FRESH CONTEXT (never reading previous review rounds)?
options: To save tokens
To avoid inheriting the writer's biases and to re-verify every citation in its real source context
Because review files are deleted after each round
Because the reviewer uses a smaller model
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because a fresh reviewer can fact-check adversarially by refetching cited sources instead of inheriting the writer's framing. Option 0 is wrong because fresh context may cost more tokens, not primarily save them. Option 2 is wrong because persisted review artifacts exist in the pipeline state; deletion is not the reason. Option 3 is wrong because the requirement is about independence and source verification, not model size.

quiz.prompt: The writer–reviewer alignment loop is bounded at 3 rounds. What happens if round 3 still ends in REVISE?
options: The chapter is auto-published
The loop restarts from zero
A human checkpoint: the pipeline stops and asks a human to decide
The orchestrator rewrites the chapter itself
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is correct because the bounded loop exits to a human checkpoint when REVISE persists at round 3. Option 0 is wrong because REVISE means the chapter is not certified for publication. Option 1 is wrong because restarting would create an unbounded self-justifying loop. Option 3 is wrong because the orchestrator coordinates state and agents; it does not take over the writer's work.

quiz.prompt: What is the main benefit of configuring LSP servers for Copilot CLI (.github/lsp.json)?
options: It enables syntax highlighting in the terminal
Compiler-grade operations like find-references return compact structured results instead of loading whole files into context
It replaces the need for Git
It makes Copilot work offline
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because LSP operations such as definitions, references, symbols, and calls return precise structured data with fewer tokens. Option 0 is wrong because syntax highlighting is an editor display feature, not the purpose of CLI LSP configuration. Option 2 is wrong because LSP augments code navigation and does not replace version control. Option 3 is wrong because LSP servers do not make Copilot's model service run offline.

quiz.prompt: Which part of an installed skill is loaded into context at EVERY turn, even when the skill never triggers?
options: The full SKILL.md body
Nothing until it triggers
The name + description frontmatter (roughly 35–300 tokens per skill)
Only the folder name
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is correct because the router must see each installed skill's name and description on every turn to decide whether it matches. Option 0 is wrong because the full body loads on demand only after a skill triggers. Option 1 is wrong because at least the routing metadata is always present. Option 3 is wrong because a folder name alone is not enough semantic information for the router.

quiz.prompt: You run your eval fixtures with_skill (9/10) and without_skill (8/10). What does the handbook conclude?
options: Ship it — 9/10 is a great score
The +10% delta is below the ~30% bar: the skill probably doesn't justify its place in context
Add more assertions until the delta grows
Rewrite the fixtures so without_skill fails
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because the handbook values the with/without delta, and +10% is below the approximate 30% threshold for keeping context. Option 0 is wrong because an absolute 9/10 can still be poor value if the baseline is already 8/10. Option 2 is wrong because adding assertions to force a better-looking delta is eval gaming. Option 3 is wrong because fixtures must reflect realistic behavior, not be rewritten to make the no-skill baseline fail.

quiz.prompt: In pairwise LLM-judge comparisons, how do you neutralize position bias?
options: Always put the candidate answer first
Use a longer rubric
Call the judge twice with the order inverted and only declare a winner if both calls agree
Raise the temperature
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is correct because running A/B and B/A and requiring agreement exposes and reduces first-position preference. Option 0 is wrong because always putting the candidate first amplifies the very bias being controlled. Option 1 is wrong because a longer rubric may clarify criteria but does not by itself remove ordering bias. Option 3 is wrong because higher temperature increases nondeterminism rather than making the verdict more reliable.

quiz.prompt: What does the handbook's single-writer interlock protect in the writing pipeline?
options: It ensures only one agent mutates persistent pipeline state at a time
It prevents the reviewer from reading source URLs
It forces every artifact to be stored as JSON
It makes the writer and reviewer share one context
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is correct because a single-writer interlock prevents competing agents from corrupting the persistent runtime state. Option 1 is wrong because the reviewer must read source URLs to fact-check. Option 2 is wrong because the pipeline can persist Markdown and other artifacts; JSON is not the core guarantee. Option 3 is wrong because the reviewer specifically needs fresh, isolated context.

quiz.prompt: Which verdict means the handbook pipeline can exit immediately with a chapter ready for human review?
options: REVISE
CERTIFY
REJECT
RESTART
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because CERTIFY is the reviewer's positive verdict that the chapter is ready for human review. Option 0 is wrong because REVISE sends the chapter back through another writer round if rounds remain. Option 2 is wrong because REJECT exits to a human checkpoint due to a blocking problem, not readiness. Option 3 is wrong because RESTART is not one of the pipeline verdicts described.

quiz.prompt: In LSP configuration for Copilot CLI, which fields are required for a server entry?
options: command and fileExtensions
args and env
name and version
repository and branch
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is correct because the CLI LSP configuration requires a command to start the server and fileExtensions to map files to language IDs. Option 1 is wrong because args and env are optional helpers, not required fields. Option 2 is wrong because name and version are not the configuration keys used to launch the LSP server. Option 3 is wrong because repository and branch describe source control, not local language-server configuration.

quiz.prompt: What is the priority order Copilot CLI uses for LSP configuration?
options: User config, then plugins, then project config
Project config, then plugins, then user config
Plugins only, unless disabled
The largest configuration file wins
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because the handbook states that .github/lsp.json in the project has priority, followed by plugin configs, then the user config. Option 0 is wrong because it reverses the precedence and would let personal settings override team settings. Option 2 is wrong because plugins are only one tier in the precedence chain. Option 3 is wrong because file size has no role in configuration priority.

quiz.prompt: When comparing APM, plugins, symlink, and third-party tools, what actually determines the fixed token tax of installed skills?
options: Whether the distribution mode is called a plugin
The scope and breadth of installation, because descriptions are always candidates
The number of Git commits in the source repository
Whether the package was installed from VS Code or a terminal
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because broadly installed skills add their descriptions to the router in more conversations, regardless of distribution mechanism. Option 0 is wrong because plugin versus APM is not the direct token determinant. Option 2 is wrong because repository history does not enter the prompt as routing metadata. Option 3 is wrong because installation UI does not change the per-turn description cost.

quiz.prompt: Which situation is best suited to APM rather than a user-scoped plugin?
options: A project needs a small, version-locked set of primitives shared by all contributors
A developer wants the same brainstorming toolkit in every workspace
A team refuses to commit any manifest or lockfile
A one-off local experiment should track HEAD manually
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is correct because APM is designed for per-project declarations with a manifest and lockfile that teams can reproduce. Option 1 is wrong because a user-scoped plugin is better for personal tooling used everywhere. Option 2 is wrong because APM's strength depends on committed apm.yml and apm.lock.yaml. Option 3 is wrong because manual HEAD tracking is closer to git clone plus symlink, not APM's reproducible model.

quiz.prompt: Why are binary eval assertions intentionally strict pass/fail checks?
options: They make results comparable across runs and expose regressions
They let the model explain partial credit
They remove the need for realistic prompts
They guarantee deterministic LLM output
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is correct because pass/fail assertions make runs comparable and regression-friendly even when LLM behavior is probabilistic. Option 1 is wrong because partial credit belongs to graded rubrics, not binary evals. Option 2 is wrong because the handbook stresses realistic prompts for useful fixtures. Option 3 is wrong because binary evals evaluate nondeterministic outputs; they do not make the model itself deterministic.

quiz.prompt: When should you move from binary evals to an LLM-judge rubric?
options: When quality dimensions like usefulness, tone, or faithfulness cannot be captured by regex-like assertions
Whenever a binary eval fails once
When you want to avoid human calibration
When the expected output must be shorter than 72 characters
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is correct because graded rubrics and LLM judges are for qualitative dimensions that pass/fail string checks cannot measure. Option 1 is wrong because a failing binary eval may simply indicate a concrete bug in a deterministic requirement. Option 2 is wrong because the handbook insists that judges need calibration against human labels. Option 3 is wrong because length constraints are exactly the kind of rule binary assertions handle well.

quiz.prompt: What makes an uncalibrated LLM judge unsafe as a metric?
options: It is an opinion that may encode position, verbosity, self-preference, and nondeterminism biases
It cannot output JSON
It can only compare code, not prose
It always costs less than binary evals
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is correct because a judge becomes a metric only after bias controls and calibration against a golden set of human labels. Option 1 is wrong because judge prompts commonly require JSON with a score and reason. Option 2 is wrong because LLM judges are specifically useful for open-ended prose and qualitative outputs. Option 3 is wrong because cost is not the safety issue, and judge evals may be more expensive than binary checks.

levels.title: Context engineering mastery
levels.focus: Token sobriety, mechanical reduction tooling, autoresearch loops, and cache-aware model orchestration.

quiz.prompt: Why does output quality degrade even on models with huge context windows?
options: Long contexts are truncated silently
Signal dilution: the model attends to every token, so more noise means less focus on what matters
Big windows disable the prompt cache
Tokens beyond 100k are free but ignored
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because a lower signal-to-noise ratio makes relevant instructions and code harder for the model to prioritize, even inside a large window. Option 0 is wrong because silent truncation is not the core phenomenon described by signal dilution. Option 2 is wrong because large context windows do not inherently disable prompt caching. Option 3 is wrong because tokens beyond an arbitrary threshold are neither free nor automatically ignored.

quiz.prompt: Which code-structuring practice most reduces the context Copilot needs to load?
options: Merging related services into one big file for fewer reads
SRP with domain-driven names: one file = one intent, e.g. calculateShippingCost(order, policy): Money
Files of at most 5 lines
Adding detailed comments on every line
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because SRP and ubiquitous language make intent visible in names and let Copilot load only the relevant unit. Option 0 is wrong because one large service increases irrelevant context and cognitive load. Option 2 is wrong because extreme fragmentation creates navigation noise and more files to inspect. Option 3 is wrong because comments can help selectively, but line-by-line commentary adds tokens and often restates the code.

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes a genuinely useful synthesis sub-agent from a fake one?
options: It uses a premium model
It reads 3 files (~4000 tokens) and returns a ~200-token conclusion instead of copy-pasting raw file contents
It always returns JSON
It runs in under 10 ms
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because a useful synthesis sub-agent compresses raw context into a decision-ready conclusion for the orchestrator. Option 0 is wrong because premium model choice does not prove any token reduction. Option 2 is wrong because JSON may structure output but does not guarantee synthesis. Option 3 is wrong because latency alone says nothing about whether the sub-agent reduced context.

quiz.prompt: In an autoresearch loop, how many changes should each experiment make to SKILL.md?
options: As many as possible to converge faster
Exactly one mutation, then re-run and KEEP or DISCARD
One per eval fixture
None — only the fixtures change
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because a single mutation is the only way to attribute a score change to a specific prompt change. Option 0 is wrong because multiple simultaneous edits make causality impossible to read. Option 2 is wrong because fixtures define tests, not the number of prompt edits to bundle. Option 3 is wrong because autoresearch optimizes SKILL.md while holding evals stable enough to compare runs.

quiz.prompt: You planned with a deep-reasoning model and now want a lighter model to implement. When is the Markdown transfer (plan.md + new session) better than forking the conversation?
options: When the implementation needs every detail of the planning reasoning
When the plan is cleanly summarizable in a document, so the new session starts with minimal, noise-free context
When you want to keep the warm cache prefix
Never — forking is always better
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because Markdown transfer preserves the actionable spec while discarding planning noise for a clean implementation session. Option 0 is wrong because needing every reasoning detail favors a fork with full inherited context. Option 2 is wrong because a new Markdown-based session starts with a cold cache, not a warm prefix. Option 3 is wrong because fork and Markdown are tradeoffs, and neither is universally superior.

quiz.prompt: In the Route & Assemble subagent pattern, which model tier should the orchestrator itself run on?
options: The premium reasoning tier — it makes the hardest decisions
The lightweight tier (e.g. Haiku 4.5 / Gemini Flash) because it only routes and assembles, never reasons deeply or writes code
The same tier as the implementer
It doesn't matter
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because the orchestrator should keep little context, delegate hard work, and assemble returned results, making a lightweight model sufficient. Option 0 is wrong because deep reasoning belongs to planner subagents, not the router. Option 2 is wrong because the implementer may need a stronger everyday engineering model than the orchestrator. Option 3 is wrong because choosing tiers by role is central to the pattern's cost and context benefits.

quiz.prompt: Which action does NOT break the prompt cache during a long session?
options: Editing an earlier message
Reinserting a large block at the top of the conversation
Appending new context at the end of the conversation
Switching models mid-session
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is correct because appending preserves the stable prefix that prompt caching can reuse. Option 0 is wrong because editing an early message changes the prefix and invalidates everything after it. Option 1 is wrong because inserting a large block upstream shifts the prompt and breaks downstream cache reuse. Option 3 is wrong because switching models undermines the one-model-per-session cache strategy.

quiz.prompt: Which four consequences of tokens does the handbook emphasize beyond simple billing?
options: Cost, latency, context saturation, and signal dilution
Syntax, types, imports, and tests
Branches, commits, tags, and releases
CPU, RAM, disk, and network
quiz.explanation: Option 0 is correct because the module frames tokens as affecting direct cost, response time, finite window occupancy, and quality through signal dilution. Option 1 is wrong because those are code concerns, not token-cost dimensions. Option 2 is wrong because version-control concepts do not describe LLM context economics. Option 3 is wrong because infrastructure resources are not the four token consequences taught in the module.

quiz.prompt: What is the recommended model-selection rule before escalating to a larger model?
options: Always start with the premium model to avoid retries
Run evals on the smallest viable model and escalate only if it fails
Choose the model with the largest context window
Use the same model for every agent to simplify operations
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because the handbook recommends proving the smallest model can pass evals before paying for a larger tier. Option 0 is wrong because defaulting to premium creates unnecessary cost and latency. Option 2 is wrong because window size alone does not guarantee quality or value. Option 3 is wrong because different agents and phases can justify different model tiers.

quiz.prompt: Why does Ubiquitous Language reduce token consumption in AI-assisted development?
options: It hides domain concepts behind shorter abbreviations
It encodes intent in names so fewer explanatory prompts and comments are needed
It forces every function to be generic
It makes the model ignore type signatures
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because names like calculateShippingCost(order, policy) carry domain meaning directly in the code. Option 0 is wrong because abbreviations often require extra explanation and increase ambiguity. Option 2 is wrong because generic functions like process(data) are exactly what need more context. Option 3 is wrong because clear type signatures help the model rather than being ignored.

quiz.prompt: In Object Calisthenics for context sobriety, why are extremely tiny five-line files discouraged?
options: They are impossible for Copilot to read
They create navigation noise and over-fragment the domain
They prevent unit tests from compiling
They force every class to be global
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because the handbook recommends coherent small units, roughly 30–80 lines, rather than fragmentation that makes the agent hop through many files. Option 0 is wrong because Copilot can read small files; the issue is too many irrelevant hops. Option 2 is wrong because file length alone does not determine whether tests compile. Option 3 is wrong because global scope is unrelated to the file-size guidance.

quiz.prompt: Which minimal-context tool is best suited to extracting a field from a large JSON file without loading the whole file?
options: ast-grep
rg
jq
tokei
quiz.explanation: Option 2 is correct because jq is designed to query JSON and extract precise fields with large token savings. Option 0 is wrong because ast-grep is for AST-based code structure and pattern matching. Option 1 is wrong because rg searches text lines but does not understand JSON structure as a query language. Option 3 is wrong because tokei reports code statistics, not JSON fields.

quiz.prompt: What does snip do in the context-reduction toolchain?
options: It rewrites source files to be shorter
It proxies shell commands and filters their output through deterministic YAML pipelines before it reaches the model
It replaces LSP servers with regex search
It stores every prompt in a public dashboard
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because snip intercepts terminal output and applies deterministic filters so verbose command results do not flood the context. Option 0 is wrong because snip filters outputs rather than modifying source code. Option 2 is wrong because snip is about shell output, not replacing compiler-grade LSP navigation. Option 3 is wrong because its stats are local; it is not a public prompt logging service.

quiz.prompt: What is the sweet spot for binary evals in an autoresearch skill loop?
options: One eval, to keep the loop fast
3 to 6 evals that are binary, specific, non-gameable, and domain-derived
Twenty or more evals so the skill memorizes the criteria
Only subjective 1–5 readability scores
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because the handbook recommends 3–6 evals with clear binary, specific, non-gameable, domain-derived checks. Option 0 is wrong because one eval rarely covers enough behavior to guide improvement. Option 2 is wrong because too many evals can make the skill recite criteria instead of improving behavior. Option 3 is wrong because subjective graded scores belong to LLM-judge rubrics, not binary autoresearch checks.

quiz.prompt: In Agent Debug Logs, why is an 88% cached-input ratio significant?
options: It means 88% of output tokens are free
It means most input tokens were served from a reused prompt prefix and the remaining uncached portion drives optimization
It proves the model made no mistakes
It means no further token reduction is possible
quiz.explanation: Option 1 is correct because cached input shows how much of the prompt prefix was reused, focusing optimization on cache breaks and new tokens. Option 0 is wrong because the ratio concerns input tokens, not output tokens. Option 2 is wrong because cache efficiency says nothing about answer correctness. Option 3 is wrong because even with a high hit rate, uncached context and output tokens can still be optimized.
